runtime_validation.meaning: This is the key point of this example: the runtime validator PASSES this case. Both quotes are real, exact, in-context text -- there is no hallucination and nothing for a source-grounding check to catch. The failure is a reasoning error, not a sourcing error, and the runtime layer has no way to detect it.

failure_category_source: experiments/E20_final_rag_test/results/E20_final_report.json's failure_taxonomy (448/576 non-Joint RAG cases fall in this category; this case was manually re-checked against that taxonomy's rule: gold_evidence_present_in_retrieved_context == true, so it is excluded from retrieval_limited by definition).
why_it_failed: The model quoted exactly the right clause (clause 9) but misread its polarity. Clause 9 is a mandatory return/destroy obligation -- the receiving party MUST return or destroy the information, full stop. The model appears to have read 'return OR destroy' as offering the receiving party a choice that implicitly permits retention in the meantime, and classified the requirement ('may retain some Confidential Information') as Entailment. The correct reading is the opposite: an unconditional return/destroy duty directly contradicts a claim that retention is permitted. This is the same systematic pattern documented in docs/experiment_registry.md's E17 entry: 9/10 of E17's C-to-E failures had evidence that overlapped the gold span -- the right clause, wrong polarity judgment -- not a missing-evidence problem.

reviewer_decision.note: This case comes from the offline E20 TEST evaluation run (2,091 cases, scored in bulk), not from a live reviewed session through the backend's reviewer decision API. In the live product, this case's needs_human_review flag and cited evidence would have been shown to a reviewer for exactly this kind of check -- the whole reason the system ships with mandatory human review rather than an automatic approval gate.
